title: The Tyger
author: William Blake

source.name: William Blake, Songs of Innocence and of Experience (1794)

text:
Tyger Tyger, burning bright,
In the forests of the night;
What immortal hand or eye,
Could frame thy fearful symmetry?

In what distant deeps or skies,
Burnt the fire of thine eyes?
On what wings dare he aspire?
What the hand, dare seize the fire?

And what shoulder, & what art,
Could twist the sinews of thy heart?
And when thy heart began to beat,
What dread hand? & what dread feet?

What the hammer? what the chain,
In what furnace was thy brain?
What the anvil? what dread grasp,
Dare its deadly terrors clasp?

When the stars threw down their spears
And water'd heaven with their tears:
Did he smile his work to see?
Did he who made the Lamb make thee?

Tyger Tyger burning bright,
In the forests of the night:
What immortal hand or eye,
Dare frame thy fearful symmetry?

masterNotes.context: Blake wrote "The Tyger" for Songs of Experience (1794), the companion volume to his earlier Songs of Innocence (1789); the two were eventually issued together as Songs of Innocence and of Experience, Shewing the Two Contrary States of the Human Soul. Blake was a printmaker as well as a poet, and he etched, hand-colored, and self-published both books rather than working through a conventional printer — the poem's original page carries his own illustration of the tiger. "The Tyger" answers, almost as a direct rebuttal, "The Lamb" from the earlier volume, in which a child asks a lamb who made it and answers confidently: God, who is also a lamb. Here the same question is asked of something fearsome, and the poem never supplies Blake's earlier easy answer. It has become one of the most anthologized poems in English, largely because it refuses to resolve its own central question.
masterNotes.form: Every stanza but the last is built entirely from questions, and Blake never answers a single one directly — the poem interrogates the tiger's maker rather than describing the tiger itself. The insistent trochaic rhythm ("TY-ger TY-ger") gives the poem a hammering, forge-like beat that matches its central conceit of the creator as blacksmith, working with hammer, chain, furnace, and anvil. The rhymed couplets tighten the pressure stanza by stanza, and the final stanza almost exactly repeats the first — except "Could frame" becomes "Dare frame," a single-word change that quietly shifts the whole poem from wonder toward something closer to accusation.
keyImages: "The forests of the night" — the tiger appears already inside a landscape charged with mystery and menace rather than lit by daylight.
The forge imagery of "the hammer," "the chain," "the anvil," and "the furnace" — the creator recast as a blacksmith laboring over something dangerous rather than a gentle craftsman.
"When the stars threw down their spears / And water'd heaven with their tears" — a cosmic image of surrender or grief whose exact meaning the poem never explains.
The final line's single altered word, "Dare frame" replacing "Could frame" — the same question returning with its emotional register changed.
whatToNotice: Notice that almost every line in the poem is a question, and count how many actually get answered.
Notice the forge vocabulary arriving in the third and fourth stanzas — hammer, chain, furnace, anvil — and what kind of maker that implies.
In the fifth stanza, notice the poem widens suddenly from the tiger's body to "the stars" and "heaven," without explanation.
Compare the first and last stanzas line by line; notice exactly which word changes.
Notice the poem never once describes the tiger's stripes, size, or behavior — only the terror and awe of imagining who could have made it.
discussionQuestions: What does it mean that Blake asks whether the same god made both "the Lamb" and the tiger, without answering?
Why might Blake choose a hammering, sing-song rhythm for a poem about something as frightening as a tiger?
Does the shift from "Could frame" to "Dare frame" change your sense of who is doing the daring — the maker, or the reader questioning the maker?
What is gained by describing the tiger entirely through the reaction it provokes, rather than through direct physical description?
furtherReading: "The Lamb" (Blake, *Songs of Innocence*) — the poem "The Tyger" is answering, asking the same question of a gentler creature.
*Songs of Innocence and of Experience* (full volume) — for the "two contrary states" frame Blake built the poem within.
Northrop Frye, *Fearful Symmetry: A Study of William Blake* — a foundational critical study that takes its title directly from this poem.

title: The Bet
author: Anton Chekhov
excerpt:
The Bet

I

It was a dark autumn night. The old banker was walking up and down his study and remembering how, fifteen years before, he had given a party one autumn evening. There had been many clever men there, and there had been interesting conversations. Among other things they had talked of capital punishment. The majority of the guests, among whom were many journalists and intellectual men, disapproved of the death penalty. They considered that form of punishment out of date, immoral, and unsuitable for Christian states. In the opinion of some of them the death penalty ought to be replaced everywhere by imprisonment for life.

“I don’t agree with you,” said their host the banker. “I have not tried either the death penalty or imprisonment for life, but if one may judge a priori, the death penalty is more moral and more humane than imprisonment for life. Capital punishment kills a man at once, but lifelong imprisonment kills him slowly. Which executioner is the more humane, he who kills you in a few minutes or he who drags the life out of you in the course of many years?”

“Both are equally immoral,” observed one of the guests, “for they both have the same object⁠—to take away life. The State is not God. It has not the right to take away what it cannot restore when it wants to.”

Among the guests was a young lawyer, a young man of five-and-twenty. When he was asked his opinion, he said:

“The death sentence and the life sentence are equally immoral, but if I had to choose between the death penalty and imprisonment for life, I would certainly choose the second. To live anyhow is better than not at all.”

A lively discussion arose. The banker, who was younger and more nervous in those days, was suddenly carried away by excitement; he struck the table with his fist and shouted at the young man:

“It’s not true! I’ll bet you two millions you wouldn’t stay in solitary confinement for five years.”

“If you mean that in earnest,” said the young man, “I’ll take the bet, but I would stay not five but fifteen years.”

“Fifteen? Done!” cried the banker. “Gentlemen, I stake two millions!”

“Agreed! You stake your millions and I stake my freedom!” said the young man.

And this wild, senseless bet was carried out! The banker, spoilt and frivolous, with millions beyond his reckoning, was delighted at the bet. At supper he made fun of the young man, and said:

“Think better of it, young man, while there is still time. To me two millions are a trifle, but you are losing three or four of the best years of your life. I say three or four, because you won’t stay longer. Don’t forget either, you unhappy man, that voluntary confinement is a great deal harder to bear than compulsory. The thought that you have the right to step out in liberty at any moment will poison your whole existence in prison. I am sorry for you.”

And now the banker, walking to and fro, remembered all this, and asked himself: “What was the object of that bet? What is the good of that man’s losing fifteen years of his life and my throwing away two millions? Can it prove that the death penalty is better or worse than imprisonment for life? No, no. It was all nonsensical and meaningless. On my part it was the caprice of a pampered man, and on his part simple greed for money.⁠ ⁠…”

Then he remembered what followed that evening. It was decided that the young man should spend the years of his captivity under the strictest supervision in one of the lodges in the banker’s garden. It was agreed that for fifteen years he should not be free to cross the threshold of the lodge, to see human beings, to hear the human voice, or to receive letters and newspapers. He was allowed to have a musical instrument and books, and was allowed to write letters, to drink wine, and to smoke. By the terms of the agreement, the only relations he could have with the outer world were by a little window made purposely for that object. He might have anything he wanted⁠—books, music, wine, and so on⁠—in any quantity he desired by writing an order, but could only receive them through the window. The agreement provided for every detail and every trifle that would make his imprisonment strictly solitary, and bound the young man to stay there exactly fifteen years, beginning from twelve o’clock of November 14, 1870, and ending at twelve o’clock of November 14, 1885. The slightest attempt on his part to break the conditions, if only two minutes before the end, released the banker from the obligation to pay him two millions.

For the first year of his confinement, as far as one could judge from his brief notes, the prisoner suffered severely from loneliness and depression. The sounds of the piano could be heard continually day and night from his lodge. He refused wine and tobacco. Wine, he wrote, excites the desires, and desires are the worst foes of the prisoner; and besides, nothing could be more dreary than drinking good wine and seeing no one. And tobacco spoilt the air of his room. In the first year the books he sent for were principally of a light character; novels with a complicated love plot, sensational and fantastic stories, and so on.

In the second year the piano was silent in the lodge, and the prisoner asked only for the classics. In the fifth year music was audible again, and the prisoner asked for wine. Those who watched him through the window said that all that year he spent doing nothing but eating and drinking and lying on his bed, frequently yawning and angrily talking to himself. He did not read books. Sometimes at night he would sit down to write; he would spend hours writing, and in the morning tear up all that he had written. More than once he could be heard crying.

In the second half of the sixth year the prisoner began zealously studying languages, philosophy, and history. He threw himself eagerly into these studies⁠—so much so that the banker had enough to do to get him the books he ordered. In the course of four years some six hundred volumes were procured at his request. It was during this period that the banker received the following letter from his prisoner:

“My dear Jailer, I write you these lines in six languages. Show them to people who know the languages. Let them read them. If they find not one mistake I implore you to fire a shot in the garden. That shot will show me that my efforts have not been thrown away. The geniuses of all ages and of all lands speak different languages, but the same flame burns in them all. Oh, if you only knew what unearthly happiness my soul feels now from being able to understand them!” The prisoner’s desire was fulfilled. The banker ordered two shots to be fired in the garden.

Then after the tenth year, the prisoner sat immovably at the table and read nothing but the Gospel. It seemed strange to the banker that a man who in four years had mastered six hundred learned volumes should waste nearly a year over one thin book easy of comprehension. Theology and histories of religion followed the Gospels.

In the last two years of his confinement the prisoner read an immense quantity of books quite indiscriminately. At one time he was busy with the natural sciences, then he would ask for Byron or Shakespeare. There were notes in which he demanded at the same time books on chemistry, and a manual of medicine, and a novel, and some treatise on philosophy or theology. His reading suggested a man swimming in the sea among the wreckage of his ship, and trying to save his life by greedily clutching first at one spar and then at another.

II

The old banker remembered all this, and thought:

“Tomorrow at twelve o’clock he will regain his freedom. By our agreement I ought to pay him two millions. If I do pay him, it is all over with me: I shall be utterly ruined.”

masterNotes.context: Chekhov wrote "The Bet" in 1889, early in a career that would make him the most influential short-story writer of his generation, at a point when he was still writing quickly for periodicals and had not yet stepped back from his medical practice. The premise is a wager struck at a dinner party: a banker and a young lawyer argue over which is crueler, a life sentence or execution, and the argument hardens into an actual bet, with the lawyer volunteering to spend fifteen years in solitary confinement to prove his point. Chekhov returned constantly, across his career, to isolation, self-deception, and the gap between what people believe about themselves and what circumstance eventually reveals. Here he uses an almost fable-like premise less as a thought experiment than as a pressure chamber for testing two men against a single, artificial constraint over a very long stretch of time.
masterNotes.form: The story is told in brisk omniscient third person, compressing fifteen years into a few pages by cutting between the banker's present-tense anxiety on the final night and quick summaries of what filtered out of the lawyer's confinement year by year, glimpsed mostly through the books he requests. Chekhov gives almost no direct access to the lawyer's interior life during the wager itself; the reader learns what he has become only secondhand, through inference and a late document, which makes the ending depend on the reader's own interpretation rather than on being told how to feel. The structure narrows steadily toward a single scene, the banker's approach to the lodge, and the story's control of pace is an early, clear demonstration of restraint as technique.
keyImages: The lodge in the banker's garden where the confinement takes place — an ordinary piece of domestic architecture repurposed into something closer to a cell, without ever losing its ordinariness.
The fifteen years reduced to a list of what the lawyer reads, request by request, so that a mind's changes are tracked entirely through its shifting appetite for books.
The banker's own fifteen years of increasingly reckless decisions outside the lodge, running in uneasy parallel to the stillness inside it.
The final approach to the lodge on the last night, staged with a hush the story has been building toward since its opening page.
whatToNotice: Notice how little direct dialogue the lawyer gets after the opening argument — his presence in the story is almost entirely mediated through what he reads and writes.
Notice the uneven pace at which years pass in the prose; some spans get a sentence, others a paragraph, tracking what the banker, and the reader, can bear to dwell on.
Notice how the opening dinner-party argument sets up two abstract positions before either man has been individually tested by anything.
Notice how sparingly Chekhov updates the physical description of the lodge over fifteen years — most of the change happens off the page.
Notice where the narration shifts from the banker's point of view toward something closer to a reported document near the close, and what that shift does to the story's authority.
discussionQuestions: The bet is framed as a debate about capital punishment, but the story becomes about something else entirely. What does it end up being about?
Why might Chekhov choose to keep the reader almost entirely outside the lawyer's confinement rather than narrating it directly?
The banker changes as much as the lawyer does over the fifteen years, in the opposite direction. What does the story gain by tracking both men?
What does the story imply about the relationship between isolation and self-knowledge — is the lawyer's transformation a gain, a loss, or something the story refuses to rank?
furtherReading: Chekhov's *Ward No. 6* — a longer, darker treatment of confinement and the porous line between keeper and kept.
Fyodor Dostoevsky's *Notes from Underground* — an earlier Russian treatment of isolation chosen rather than imposed, useful for comparison of tone and conclusion.
The other stories in the same Standard Ebooks Constance Garnett collection, for tracing how Chekhov's method changed across a decade of story writing.

title: The Story of an Hour
author: Kate Chopin
text:
The Dream of an Hour

Knowing that Mrs. Mallard was afflicted with a heart trouble, great care was taken to break to her as gently as possible the news of her husband’s death.

It was her sister Josephine who told her, in broken sentences; veiled hints that revealed in half concealing. Her husband’s friend Richards was there, too, near her. It was he who had been in the newspaper office when intelligence of the railroad disaster was received, with Brently Mallard’s name leading the list of “killed.” He had only taken the time to assure himself of its truth by a second telegram, and had hastened to forestall any less careful, less tender friend in bearing the sad message.

She did not hear the story as many women have heard the same, with a paralyzed inability to accept its significance. She wept at once, with sudden, wild abandonment, in her sister’s arms. When the storm of grief had spent itself she went away to her room alone. She would have no one follow her.

There stood, facing the open window, a comfortable, roomy armchair. Into this she sank, pressed down by a physical exhaustion that haunted her body and seemed to reach into her soul.

She could see in the open square before her house the tops of trees that where all aquiver with the new spring life. The delicious breath of rain was in the air. In the street below a peddler was crying his wares. The notes of a distant song which someone was singing reached her faintly, and countless sparrows were twittering in the eaves.

There were patches of blue sky showing here and there through the clouds that had met and piled one above the other in the west facing her window.

She sat with her head thrown back upon the cushion of the chair, quite motionless, except when a sob came up into her throat and shook her, as a child who has cried itself to sleep continues to sob in its dreams.

She was young, with a fair, calm face, whose lines bespoke repression and even a certain strength. But now there was a dull stare in her eyes, whose gaze was fixed away off yonder on one of those patches of blue sky. It was not a glance of reflection, but rather indicated a suspension of intelligent thought.

There was something coming to her and she was waiting for it, fearfully. What was it? She did not know; it was too subtle and elusive to name. But she felt it creeping out of the sky, reaching toward her through the sounds, the scents, the color that filled the air.

Now her bosom rose and fell tumultuously. She was beginning to recognize this thing that was approaching to possess her, and she was striving to beat it back with her will⁠—as powerless as her two white slender hands would have been.

When she abandoned herself a little whispered word escaped her slightly parted lips. She said it over and over under her breath: “free, free, free!” The vacant stare and the look of terror that had followed it went from her eyes. They stayed keen and bright. Her pulses beat fast, and the coursing blood warmed and relaxed every inch of her body.

She did not stop to ask if it were or were not a monstrous joy that held her. A clear and exalted perception enabled her to dismiss the suggestion as trivial.

She knew that she would weep again when she saw the kind, tender hands folded in death; the face that had never looked save with love upon her, fixed and gray and dead. But she saw beyond that bitter moment a long procession of years to come that would belong to her absolutely. And she opened and spread her arms out to them in welcome.

There would be no one to live for during those coming years; she would live for herself. There would be no powerful will bending hers in that blind persistence with which men and women believe they have a right to impose a private will upon a fellow creature. A kind intention or a cruel intention made the act seem no less a crime as she looked upon it in that brief moment of illumination.

And yet she had loved him⁠—sometimes. Often she had not. What did it matter? What could love, the unsolved mystery, count for in face of this possession of self-assertion which she suddenly recognized as the strongest impulse of her being!

“Free! Body and soul free!” she kept whispering.

Josephine was kneeling before the closed door with her lips to the keyhole, imploring for admission. “Louise, open the door! I beg; open the door⁠—you will make yourself ill. What are you doing, Louise? For heaven’s sake open the door.”

“Go away. I am not making myself ill.” No; she was drinking in a very elixir of life through that open window.

How fancy was running riot along those days ahead of her. Spring days, and summer days, and all sorts of days that would be her own. She breathed a quick prayer that life might be long. It was only yesterday she had thought with a shudder that life might be long, and now what a change.

She arose at length and opened the door to her sister’s importunities. There was a feverish triumph in her eyes, and she carried herself unwittingly like the goddess of Victory. She clasped her sister’s waist, and together they descended the stairs. Richard stood waiting for them at the bottom.

Someone was opening the front door with a latch key. It was Brently Mallard who entered, a little travel-stained, composedly carrying his gripsack and umbrella. He had been far from the scene of accident, and did not even know there had been one. He stood amazed at Josephine’s piercing cry; at Richard’s quick motion to screen him from the view of his wife, who just then looked up.

But Richard was too late.

When the doctors came they said she had died of heart disease⁠—of joy that kills.

masterNotes.context: Kate Chopin wrote "The Story of an Hour" in April 1894, by her own account in a single sitting, at a point when she had already published a novel and was building a reputation through short fiction placed in national magazines. It appeared first in Vogue that December under the title "The Dream of an Hour," a magazine whose readers skewed toward exactly the kind of comfortable, married women the story addresses. Chopin was writing in St. Louis some years after her husband's death had left her, unusually for the period, both a widow and financially independent, and her fiction returned often to the private interior of women's married lives, a subject American magazine fiction rarely treated without moralizing. The story runs only a few pages, and that compression is deliberate: Chopin allows herself almost no room for a slow build.
masterNotes.form: Told in close third person centered on Louise Mallard, the story is organized around a single hour, opening with news delivered to her and closing before that hour has fully elapsed. Chopin uses short paragraphs and a restrained, almost clinical narrating voice for material that is anything but clinical, letting the gap between tone and content do much of the work. The middle section shifts from external event into an extended interior passage that follows a feeling arriving in Louise before she has language for it — the narration tracks sensation first and supplies the word only afterward, a sequencing that mirrors how the feeling overtakes her. The story's final turn depends on ironic structure rather than plot mechanics, and rereading it changes what every earlier sentence seems to mean.
keyImages: The open window Louise sits before after the news arrives, and the ordinary spring scene beyond it — treetops, peddler's cries, patches of blue sky — deliberately full of life at a moment the story marks as about death.
The description of Louise's body in the armchair, given as pure physical sensation before the story tells us anything about what she is feeling.
A single recurring word arriving in the interior passage before Louise can consciously admit it to herself.
The staircase and the door in the story's closing scene, staged with an almost theatrical precision.
whatToNotice: Notice exactly where the narration names Louise's feeling versus where it only describes physical sensation — track the lag between body and word.
Notice how much natural, springtime imagery is packed into a story ostensibly about grief, and ask what work that imagery is doing.
Notice the story's use of interruption — how often a thought or sentence is cut off mid-course in the interior section.
Notice how briskly the opening paragraph moves through the delivery of the news itself, compared to how slowly the story lingers afterward.
Notice the very last paragraph's clinical, detached diction, and how sharply it contrasts with everything the reader now knows.
discussionQuestions: Chopin gives the reader access to Louise's interior life but almost none to anyone else's. What does the story lose, or gain, by that imbalance?
How does the story's tight time frame, a single hour, shape what Chopin is able to do with irony that a longer span wouldn't allow?
The story never states outright what kind of marriage the Mallards had. What details does Chopin give the reader to work with instead?
Is the ending a judgment on marriage in general, on this particular marriage, or on something else altogether?
furtherReading: Chopin's *The Awakening* — a novel-length treatment of the same tension between a woman's inner life and the social role of wife.
Charlotte Perkins Gilman's "The Yellow Wallpaper" — a near-contemporary American story using a woman's confined interior state to comparable, though very differently paced, effect.
Per Seyersted's *Kate Chopin: A Critical Biography* — background on the magazine culture Chopin was writing into.

Search Copper Canyon Press for this collection

masterNotes.context: Clifton published "won't you celebrate with me" in *The Book of Light* (1993), well into a career that had already produced more than a dozen collections and two National Book Award nominations before she won the award outright in 2000. She grew up in Depew, New York, the descendant of a family who had preserved an oral history reaching back to an enslaved ancestor, and Clifton wrote often, though rarely directly, out of that inheritance. Her poems are almost never capitalized and use minimal punctuation, a signature style she maintained across four decades. This poem addresses the reader directly, asking for celebration rather than sympathy, and it has become one of her most frequently taught poems, especially for how plainly it names the specific conditions — race, gender, lack of precedent — that shaped the life it describes.
masterNotes.form: The poem is built as unrhymed, unpunctuated free verse, with even the personal pronoun "i" kept lowercase — Clifton refuses grammatical convention its usual deference throughout her work. A central image compresses the poem's argument about self-invention into a handful of words, comparing the space the speaker has made a life in to a bridge between two very different registers, the exalted and the ordinary. The poem builds toward its ending through direct address and accumulating clauses rather than metaphor, and its final short statement lands harder for arriving without any rhetorical flourish to cushion it.
keyImages: The poem naming its own starting conditions — birth into a hostile environment, and both a racial and gender identity that offered no ready model — without complaint or elaboration.
The central bridge image, self-invention pictured as a precarious position between the exalted and the ordinary.
A closing gesture of self-sufficiency, one hand holding the other, pictured as a literal, almost defiant, physical act.
whatToNotice: Notice the lowercase style throughout — even the poem's one first-person pronoun refuses standard capitalization.
Notice the poem is framed as an invitation to celebrate, rather than as a statement seeking sympathy.
Notice how flatly the final statement is delivered — no exclamation, just plain assertion.
Notice that place names and proper nouns are also kept lowercase, treated as conditions rather than as specific, capitalized places.
discussionQuestions: What is the effect of framing survival as something to celebrate rather than simply endure?
Why might Clifton refuse capitalization throughout, including on the first-person pronoun?
What does the bridge image suggest about how the speaker understands her own life?
furtherReading: "homage to my hips" (Clifton) — for the same unapologetic, plainspoken celebration of self in a different register.
*Blessing the Boats: New and Selected Poems* (Clifton) — the National Book Award–winning collection spanning her career.

title: I'm Nobody! Who are you?
author: Emily Dickinson
text:
I'm Nobody! Who are you?
Are you – Nobody – too?
Then there's a pair of us!
Don't tell! they'd advertise – you know!

How dreary – to be – Somebody!
How public – like a Frog –
To tell one's name – the livelong June –
To an admiring Bog!

externalLinks.label: Search Poetry Foundation for this poem

masterNotes.context: Dickinson wrote this poem around 1861, in the same extraordinarily productive early-1860s stretch that produced most of her best-known work, though almost none of it was published in her lifetime — she kept the poems hand-sewn into small booklets, called fascicles, discovered only after her death in 1886. She lived quietly in Amherst, Massachusetts, seeing few visitors in her later years, and "nobody" and "somebody" recur across her poems as a private vocabulary for social visibility and its costs. This poem's tone is playful rather than mournful, closer to a shared joke between the speaker and an imagined reader than a complaint. It has become one of her most quoted poems, often stripped of context and treated as a simple defense of introversion, though its second stanza is considerably sharper than that reading allows.
masterNotes.form: The poem is built as a conspiratorial address — "Are you – Nobody – too?" — that recruits the reader as a co-conspirator within four lines, before the second stanza turns from intimacy to mockery. Dickinson's dashes do their usual work of controlling breath and emphasis rather than following grammatical rules, isolating "Nobody" and "Somebody" almost as proper nouns. The extended metaphor in the second stanza — a frog announcing itself to a bog all summer — lands as satire of self-importance, and the shift from the private "us" of the first stanza to the public spectacle of the second is where the poem's real argument lives.
keyImages: The pairing "Then there's a pair of us!" — instant, almost giddy solidarity built from shared anonymity.
The frog "telling one's name" to "an admiring Bog" all "the livelong June" — self-announcement recast as absurd noise nobody needed.
The capitalized "Nobody" and "Somebody" — Dickinson treats social status as if it were a formal title one could hold.
whatToNotice: Notice how quickly the poem moves from private confidence ("Don't tell!") to public satire (the frog) across just two stanzas.
Notice that "Nobody" is capitalized throughout, turning an absence of status into its own kind of identity.
Count the dashes in the first stanza and see where they fall relative to the line's grammar — they rarely land where a comma would.
Notice the exclamation points: the poem's two strongest feelings, secrecy and disdain, both get one.
discussionQuestions: Is the speaker's claim to "Nobody" status entirely sincere, or is there some pride hiding inside the modesty?
What is the effect of comparing public self-announcement to a frog's croaking rather than to another person?
Why might Dickinson end on mockery of "Somebody" rather than on the earlier warmth of "there's a pair of us"?
furtherReading: "Because I could not stop for Death" (Dickinson) — for the same dash-driven meter turned toward a much graver subject.
Helen Vendler, *Dickinson: Selected Poems and Commentaries* — includes a close reading of this poem's shift in tone between stanzas.

title: We Wear the Mask
author: Paul Laurence Dunbar

source.name: Paul Laurence Dunbar, Majors and Minors (1895)

text:
We wear the mask that grins and lies,
It hides our cheeks and shades our eyes,—
This debt we pay to human guile;
With torn and bleeding hearts we smile,
And mouth with myriad subtleties.

Why should the world be over-wise,
In counting all our tears and sighs?
Nay, let them only see us, while
      We wear the mask.

We smile, but, O great Christ, our cries
To thee from tortured souls arise.
We sing, but oh the clay is vile
Beneath our feet, and long the mile;
But let the world dream otherwise,
      We wear the mask!

externalLinks.label: Search Poetry Foundation for this poem

masterNotes.context: Dunbar published "We Wear the Mask" in 1895, in the collection *Majors and Minors*, three decades after the end of slavery and squarely within the era of Jim Crow segregation and the rollback of Reconstruction-era rights. He was the first African American poet to achieve a major national literary reputation, praised by William Dean Howells, though Howells's introduction to Dunbar's next book pushed him toward dialect poems at the expense of the formal, standard-English verse this poem represents — a tension Dunbar resented throughout his career. "We Wear the Mask" is written in that formal register, a rondeau borrowed from French verse tradition, and it speaks in a collective "we" rather than through a single character. It remains one of the most frequently taught and anthologized poems about the psychological cost of concealment under oppression.
masterNotes.form: The poem is a rondeau, a French form built on a refrain — "We wear the mask" — that closes each stanza and returns, slightly altered, as the poem's final words. That formal borrowing matters: Dunbar shows complete command of a demanding European verse form while writing about a mask forced onto Black Americans by a white audience unwilling to see past it. The poem's central irony sits in its own performance — a poem about hidden suffering that is itself formally poised and controlled, never breaking into the "torn and bleeding" register it describes. The direct address to "great Christ" in the final stanza is the poem's one break from its outward composure, a private cry the mask is explicitly not meant to show.
keyImages: "The mask that grins and lies" — a face deliberately built to perform an emotion it does not feel.
"With torn and bleeding hearts we smile" — the poem's central juxtaposition, agony and pleasant expression forced into the same line.
"O great Christ, our cries / To thee from tortured souls arise" — the one moment the mask is explicitly dropped, and only toward heaven, not toward the world.
whatToNotice: Notice the poem is spoken in "we," never "I" — the mask belongs to a whole community, not a single speaker.
Notice how formally controlled the poem's own language is, even while describing torn hearts and tortured souls.
Notice where the refrain "We wear the mask" falls in each stanza, and how its meaning shifts by the final exclamation point.
Notice that the poem never shows us what is underneath the mask directly — only that something is.
discussionQuestions: What does it mean that the poem's one moment of unmasked feeling is addressed to Christ rather than to the reader?
Why might Dunbar have chosen a tightly formal French verse structure to write about concealment and pain?
Does the collective "we" make the poem's argument more powerful, or does it flatten individual experience?
furtherReading: Dunbar's dialect poems (e.g. "When Malindy Sings") — for the contrasting register Dunbar was pushed toward and sometimes resisted.
Paul Laurence Dunbar, *Lyrics of Lowly Life* — the 1896 collection that made this poem widely known.

title: The Awakening
author: Kate Chopin
excerpt:
I

A green and yellow parrot, which hung in a cage outside the door, kept repeating over and over:

“Allez vous-en! Allez vous-en! Sapristi! That’s all right!”

He could speak a little Spanish, and also a language which nobody understood, unless it was the mockingbird that hung on the other side of the door, whistling his fluty notes out upon the breeze with maddening persistence.

Mr. Pontellier, unable to read his newspaper with any degree of comfort, arose with an expression and an exclamation of disgust.

He walked down the gallery and across the narrow “bridges” which connected the Lebrun cottages one with the other. He had been seated before the door of the main house. The parrot and the mockingbird were the property of Madame Lebrun, and they had the right to make all the noise they wished. Mr. Pontellier had the privilege of quitting their society when they ceased to be entertaining.

He stopped before the door of his own cottage, which was the fourth one from the main building and next to the last. Seating himself in a wicker rocker which was there, he once more applied himself to the task of reading the newspaper. The day was Sunday; the paper was a day old. The Sunday papers had not yet reached Grand Isle. He was already acquainted with the market reports, and he glanced restlessly over the editorials and bits of news which he had not had time to read before quitting New Orleans the day before.

Mr. Pontellier wore eyeglasses. He was a man of forty, of medium height and rather slender build; he stooped a little. His hair was brown and straight, parted on one side. His beard was neatly and closely trimmed.

Once in a while he withdrew his glance from the newspaper and looked about him. There was more noise than ever over at the house. The main building was called “the house,” to distinguish it from the cottages. The chattering and whistling birds were still at it. Two young girls, the Farival twins, were playing a duet from Zampa upon the piano. Madame Lebrun was bustling in and out, giving orders in a high key to a yard-boy whenever she got inside the house, and directions in an equally high voice to a dining-room servant whenever she got outside. She was a fresh, pretty woman, clad always in white with elbow sleeves. Her starched skirts crinkled as she came and went. Farther down, before one of the cottages, a lady in black was walking demurely up and down, telling her beads. A good many persons of the pension had gone over to the Chénière Caminada in Beaudelet’s lugger to hear mass. Some young people were out under the water oaks playing croquet. Mr. Pontellier’s two children were there⁠—sturdy little fellows of four and five. A quadroon nurse followed them about with a faraway, meditative air.

Mr. Pontellier finally lit a cigar and began to smoke, letting the paper drag idly from his hand. He fixed his gaze upon a white sunshade that was advancing at snail’s pace from the beach. He could see it plainly between the gaunt trunks of the water oaks and across the stretch of yellow camomile. The gulf looked far away, melting hazily into the blue of the horizon. The sunshade continued to approach slowly. Beneath its pink-lined shelter were his wife, Mrs. Pontellier, and young Robert Lebrun. When they reached the cottage, the two seated themselves with some appearance of fatigue upon the upper step of the porch, facing each other, each leaning against a supporting post.

“What folly! to bathe at such an hour in such heat!” exclaimed Mr. Pontellier. He himself had taken a plunge at daylight. That was why the morning seemed long to him.

“You are burnt beyond recognition,” he added, looking at his wife as one looks at a valuable piece of personal property which has suffered some damage. She held up her hands, strong, shapely hands, and surveyed them critically, drawing up her fawn sleeves above the wrists. Looking at them reminded her of her rings, which she had given to her husband before leaving for the beach. She silently reached out to him, and he, understanding, took the rings from his vest pocket and dropped them into her open palm. She slipped them upon her fingers; then clasping her knees, she looked across at Robert and began to laugh. The rings sparkled upon her fingers. He sent back an answering smile.

“What is it?” asked Pontellier, looking lazily and amused from one to the other. It was some utter nonsense; some adventure out there in the water, and they both tried to relate it at once. It did not seem half so amusing when told. They realized this, and so did Mr. Pontellier. He yawned and stretched himself. Then he got up, saying he had half a mind to go over to Klein’s hotel and play a game of billiards.

“Come go along, Lebrun,” he proposed to Robert. But Robert admitted quite frankly that he preferred to stay where he was and talk to Mrs. Pontellier.

“Well, send him about his business when he bores you, Edna,” instructed her husband as he prepared to leave.

“Here, take the umbrella,” she exclaimed, holding it out to him. He accepted the sunshade, and lifting it over his head descended the steps and walked away.

“Coming back to dinner?” his wife called after him. He halted a moment and shrugged his shoulders. He felt in his vest pocket; there was a ten-dollar bill there. He did not know; perhaps he would return for the early dinner and perhaps he would not. It all depended upon the company which he found over at Klein’s and the size of “the game.” He did not say this, but she understood it, and laughed, nodding goodbye to him.

Both children wanted to follow their father when they saw him starting out. He kissed them and promised to bring them back bonbons and peanuts.

masterNotes.context: Chopin published *The Awakening* in 1899, late in a career built mostly on short fiction set among the Creole and Cajun communities of Louisiana, where she had lived as a young wife. The novel's frank treatment of a married woman's sexual and artistic self-discovery drew hostile reviews on release, and some libraries removed it from circulation; Chopin herself published almost nothing else before her death five years later. It fell out of print for decades and was effectively rediscovered in the 1960s and 70s, when feminist critics and scholars of American realism restored it to the canon, and it is now a fixture of American literature anthologies and university syllabi. The Gulf Coast resort of Grand Isle, where much of the novel opens, was a real seasonal retreat for well-off New Orleans families, and Chopin renders its heat, water, and leisure with the same close naturalist attention Guy de Maupassant, a writer she admired and translated, brought to French provincial life.
masterNotes.form: Chopin writes in a close but not fully interior third person, following Edna Pontellier's perceptions while withholding easy access to her reasoning, so that the reader often understands an impulse a beat before Edna names it to herself. Short, scene-based chapters replace continuous narrative summary, each one built around a single setting or conversation rather than a stretch of elapsed time. The prose favors concrete sensory detail, especially sound and water imagery, over authorial commentary or moral framing, which was itself part of what scandalized contemporary reviewers: the novel declines to judge its protagonist.
keyImages: Edna's early, halting attempts to swim at Grand Isle, described as much through the sensation of the water as through the act itself — the novel's clearest early image of a body learning what it wants.
The recurring sound of the sea, returned to at intervals throughout the book, described less as scenery than as something that seems to speak directly to Edna.
Adèle Ratignolle's hands at the piano and Mademoiselle Reisz's playing, set against each other as two entirely different models of what a woman's art and attention can look like.
The Pontellier house on Esplanade Street, and Edna's small, specific acts of withdrawal from its social rituals, which register as radical precisely because they are so quiet.
whatToNotice: Notice how often Edna's feelings are introduced through physical sensation — fatigue, heat, the pull of water — before the narration supplies any interpretation of them.

Notice the contrast Chopin builds between Adèle Ratignolle and Mademoiselle Reisz in the novel's early chapters, and how each woman represents a different, incomplete answer to what Edna might become.
Pay attention to what Léonce Pontellier notices and fails to notice about his wife in the opening chapters — his attention is a measuring instrument the novel uses on Edna without her consent.
Notice how rarely the narrator explains Edna's motives in full sentences of psychological explanation, compared to how much space is given to setting and gesture.
Track the recurrence of music in the early chapters and how differently each character listens to it.
discussionQuestions: What does Chopin's refusal to moralize about Edna's choices ask of the reader, compared to a novel that took a clearer stance?
How do Adèle Ratignolle and Mademoiselle Reisz function as two different models of womanhood that Edna is measured against, and against which she measures herself?
Why might Chopin have chosen the sea as the novel's dominant recurring image rather than a domestic or urban one?
What does the novel suggest about the relationship between artistic ambition and the domestic roles available to a woman like Edna in this setting?
furtherReading: Kate Chopin's short story "The Story of an Hour" — a much shorter treatment of a wife's inner life in a moment of sudden, unlooked-for freedom.
Gustave Flaubert's *Madame Bovary* — an earlier novel Chopin knew well, working similar territory of a woman's dissatisfaction with a respectable marriage.
Per Seyersted's biography *Kate Chopin: A Critical Biography* — the study most responsible for the novel's mid-century critical recovery.

masterNotes.context: Ishiguro published *The Remains of the Day* in 1989, his third novel, and it won the Booker Prize that year; he received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2017. The novel is narrated by Stevens, an English butler, in the form of a journal kept during a brief motoring trip through the West Country in 1956, a framing device that lets Ishiguro set Stevens's account of a single week against decades of service at Darlington Hall recalled in retrospect. The country-house setting and the interwar period Stevens repeatedly circles back to draw on a long English literary tradition of upstairs-downstairs fiction, which the novel uses while quietly working against its usual assumptions about whose account of events should be trusted. The book was adapted into a widely seen 1993 film, which considerably widened its readership beyond the audience for literary fiction.
masterNotes.form: The novel is written entirely in Stevens's first-person voice, formal, self-monitoring, and given to abstraction exactly where feeling threatens to surface, so that the gap between what Stevens reports and what the reader infers becomes the book's primary source of meaning. The journal-entry structure lets present-tense travel observations trigger extended retrospective digressions with only light transitions, blurring 1956 and the 1920s-30s almost as freely as *Beloved* blurs its own past and present, though to very different ends. Ishiguro sustains dramatic irony throughout by keeping Stevens's professional vocabulary of "dignity" and "greatness" stable even as the events he recounts increasingly strain it.
keyImages: Stevens's repeated, almost theoretical discussions of what makes a butler "great," returned to at intervals as his private measure of a life well spent.
The now much-diminished staff at Darlington Hall under its new American owner, a small but persistent reminder of how much has already ended before the narration begins.
Miss Kenton's letter, which prompts Stevens's journey, read and reread by him for meanings he seems reluctant to state plainly.
The view from a Salisbury hillside partway through the trip, offered by a stranger as an image of English landscape's quiet, unspectacular greatness — a claim the novel lets sit uncommented on.
whatToNotice: Notice how often Stevens explains or justifies a feeling in professional terms just after a moment that seems to call for a personal one.
Notice the vocabulary Stevens uses to define "dignity" and "greatness," and track whether it stays consistent as the journey continues.
Pay attention to what Stevens chooses to report about his former employer, Lord Darlington, and what he declines to evaluate directly.
Notice the ordinary strangers Stevens meets on his trip, and how each conversation quietly tests a claim he has made about himself.
Track the handful of moments Stevens describes his own physical or emotional state without a professional framing, and notice how rare they are.
discussionQuestions: What does Stevens's vocabulary of "dignity" and professional "greatness" allow him to avoid saying directly, and where does that strategy start to fail?
How does the frame of a short present-day journey change how you read the much longer stretch of remembered past it keeps interrupting?
What responsibility, if any, does the novel suggest Stevens bears for decisions made by Lord Darlington that he merely served?
How does the novel use ordinary strangers Stevens meets on the road to test or unsettle his own account of himself?
furtherReading: Kazuo Ishiguro's *Never Let Me Go* — another novel built on a narrator whose calm, controlled voice conceals more than it states.
P. G. Wodehouse's Jeeves stories — an earlier, comic use of the English butler figure that this novel's premise quietly answers.
Ishiguro's Nobel Prize lecture, "My Twentieth Century Evening and Other Small Breakthroughs" — his own account of the concerns running through his fiction.

masterNotes.context: "Interpreter of Maladies" is the title story of Jhumpa Lahiri's first collection, published by Houghton Mifflin in 1999, which went on to win the Pulitzer Prize for Fiction in 2000, making Lahiri the first writer of South Asian descent to receive it. Lahiri was born in London to Bengali parents and raised in Rhode Island, and much of her early fiction, this story included, works the territory between Indian-American family life and the experience of visiting India as a partial outsider. The story follows an Indian-American family being driven around Indian tourist sites by a local guide who also works, in his other job, as a translator for a doctor treating patients who speak a different regional language than he does — a detail the collection's title borrows directly. Lahiri's prose in this period is plain and controlled, more interested in what goes unsaid between people who technically share a language than in overt drama.
masterNotes.form: The story is told in close third person centered on Mr. Kapasi, the guide, which is a deliberate choice — the tourists he is driving are the ostensible subject, but the reader experiences the day's events refracted through his hopes and misreadings rather than theirs. Lahiri paces the story as a single day's excursion, structured around stops at tourist sites that double as settings for the shifting dynamic between Mr. Kapasi and one of the visiting family's parents. Dialogue in the story is often oblique, characters answering questions other than the ones asked, and Lahiri lets physical detail, what people wear, eat, photograph, carry information the characters never state directly. The story's ending resists a clean resolution, closing on an image rather than an explanation.
keyImages: Mr. Kapasi's business card, which he hands over early in the story and which becomes freighted with more meaning to him than to the family he gives it to.
The family's mismatched relationship to the country they are visiting, visible in small choices about food, dress, and what they choose to photograph.
The temple carvings the family stops to see partway through the day, treated by the tour itself as background rather than destination.
A piece of paper exchanged partway through the story, whose significance depends entirely on what has and hasn't been said aloud around it.
whatToNotice: Notice how often Mr. Kapasi's internal narration diverges from what he actually says to the family in the car.
Notice the details Lahiri gives about each family member's clothing and manner, and what those details communicate about their relationship to India and to each other.
Notice how the story paces its stops at tourist sites, and how each stop shifts the dynamic between Mr. Kapasi and the parent he is drawn to slightly further.
Notice the story's handling of Mr. Kapasi's other job, the actual interpreting of maladies, and how sparingly Lahiri returns to it once it's introduced.
Notice how the final scene is staged physically, who is standing where, what passes between which characters, rather than explained.
discussionQuestions: Mr. Kapasi imagines a version of his relationship with one of the visiting family's parents that the story lets the reader see is at least partly mistaken. Where exactly does that misreading begin?
How does the story use the family's status as tourists, seeing India as outsiders, to complicate what "interpreting" means in the title?
What does the story suggest about the limits of language even between people who technically share one?
Why might Lahiri choose to center the story on Mr. Kapasi's perspective rather than the visiting family's?
furtherReading: Lahiri's *The Namesake* — a novel expanding on the same territory of Indian-American identity across generations.
Other stories in the *Interpreter of Maladies* collection, particularly "A Temporary Matter," for a companion treatment of what goes unsaid inside a marriage.
The 2000 Pulitzer Prize citation and contemporary reviews of the collection, useful for the reception context around its unusually fast critical and popular success.

title: Anna Karenina
author: Leo Tolstoy
form: novel, translated from Russian by Constance Garnett
excerpt:
I

Happy families are all alike; every unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.

Everything was in confusion in the Oblonskys’ house. The wife had discovered that the husband was carrying on an intrigue with a French girl, who had been a governess in their family, and she had announced to her husband that she could not go on living in the same house with him. This position of affairs had now lasted three days, and not only the husband and wife themselves, but all the members of their family and household, were painfully conscious of it. Every person in the house felt that there was no sense in their living together, and that the stray people brought together by chance in any inn had more in common with one another than they, the members of the family and household of the Oblonskys. The wife did not leave her own room, the husband had not been at home for three days. The children ran wild all over the house; the English governess quarreled with the housekeeper, and wrote to a friend asking her to look out for a new situation for her; the man-cook had walked off the day before just at dinner time; the kitchen-maid, and the coachman had given warning.

Three days after the quarrel, Prince Stepan Arkadyevitch Oblonsky⁠—Stiva, as he was called in the fashionable world⁠—woke up at his usual hour, that is, at eight o’clock in the morning, not in his wife’s bedroom, but on the leather-covered sofa in his study. He turned over his stout, well-cared-for person on the springy sofa, as though he would sink into a long sleep again; he vigorously embraced the pillow on the other side and buried his face in it; but all at once he jumped up, sat up on the sofa, and opened his eyes.

“Yes, yes, how was it now?” he thought, going over his dream. “Now, how was it? To be sure! Alabin was giving a dinner at Darmstadt; no, not Darmstadt, but something American. Yes, but then, Darmstadt was in America. Yes, Alabin was giving a dinner on glass tables, and the tables sang, Il mio tesoro⁠—not Il mio tesoro though, but something better, and there were some sort of little decanters on the table, and they were women, too,” he remembered.

Stepan Arkadyevitch’s eyes twinkled gaily, and he pondered with a smile. “Yes, it was nice, very nice. There was a great deal more that was delightful, only there’s no putting it into words, or even expressing it in one’s thoughts awake.” And noticing a gleam of light peeping in beside one of the serge curtains, he cheerfully dropped his feet over the edge of the sofa, and felt about with them for his slippers, a present on his last birthday, worked for him by his wife on gold-colored morocco. And, as he had done every day for the last nine years, he stretched out his hand, without getting up, towards the place where his dressing-gown always hung in his bedroom. And thereupon he suddenly remembered that he was not sleeping in his wife’s room, but in his study, and why: the smile vanished from his face, he knitted his brows.

“Ah, ah, ah! Oo!⁠ ⁠…” he muttered, recalling everything that had happened. And again every detail of his quarrel with his wife was present to his imagination, all the hopelessness of his position, and worst of all, his own fault.

“Yes, she won’t forgive me, and she can’t forgive me. And the most awful thing about it is that it’s all my fault⁠—all my fault, though I’m not to blame. That’s the point of the whole situation,” he reflected. “Oh, oh, oh!” he kept repeating in despair, as he remembered the acutely painful sensations caused him by this quarrel.

Most unpleasant of all was the first minute when, on coming, happy and good-humored, from the theater, with a huge pear in his hand for his wife, he had not found his wife in the drawing-room, to his surprise had not found her in the study either, and saw her at last in her bedroom with the unlucky letter that revealed everything in her hand.

She, his Dolly, forever fussing and worrying over household details, and limited in her ideas, as he considered, was sitting perfectly still with the letter in her hand, looking at him with an expression of horror, despair, and indignation.

“What’s this? this?” she asked, pointing to the letter.

And at this recollection, Stepan Arkadyevitch, as is so often the case, was not so much annoyed at the fact itself as at the way in which he had met his wife’s words.

There happened to him at that instant what does happen to people when they are unexpectedly caught in something very disgraceful. He did not succeed in adapting his face to the position in which he was placed towards his wife by the discovery of his fault. Instead of being hurt, denying, defending himself, begging forgiveness, instead of remaining indifferent even⁠—anything would have been better than what he did do⁠—his face utterly involuntarily (reflex spinal action, reflected Stepan Arkadyevitch, who was fond of physiology)⁠—utterly involuntarily assumed its habitual, good-humored, and therefore idiotic smile.

This idiotic smile he could not forgive himself. Catching sight of that smile, Dolly shuddered as though at physical pain, broke out with her characteristic heat into a flood of cruel words, and rushed out of the room. Since then she had refused to see her husband.

“It’s that idiotic smile that’s to blame for it all,” thought Stepan Arkadyevitch.

“But what’s to be done? What’s to be done?” he said to himself in despair, and found no answer.

masterNotes.context: Tolstoy serialized *Anna Karenina* in the journal *The Russian Messenger* between 1875 and 1877, publishing it as a complete novel in 1878. He wrote it in the years after finishing *War and Peace*, while his own religious and moral preoccupations were sharpening toward the crisis that would reshape his later life and writing. Constance Garnett produced this translation in the early 1900s, part of a prolific career that first made the great Russian realists broadly available to English readers; because Garnett died in 1946, her translation of the novel has itself long since entered the public domain on both sides of the Atlantic, distinct from the question of the original Russian text's own public-domain status. The novel is usually read alongside *War and Peace* as one of the two works that established Tolstoy's reputation as a novelist of the first rank, and it remains a staple of world-literature courses and Russian-literature curricula.
masterNotes.form: Tolstoy alternates between two loosely connected plot strands, following Anna's household and Konstantin Levin's in turn, a structure that lets the novel compare very different answers to questions of marriage, faith, and how to live, without ever forcing the two strands into a single unified plot. The narration moves fluidly between an omniscient vantage and close access to individual characters' half-formed thoughts, an early and influential use of what would later be called free indirect style. Tolstoy's chapters are short relative to the novel's total length, each usually confined to a single scene, which gives even this very long book a scene-by-scene, almost cinematic pace rather than the density of continuous summary.
keyImages: The bustle and disorder of the Oblonsky household in the opening chapters, introduced before either Anna or Levin appears, establishing domestic disruption as the novel's first subject.
The Moscow train station where Anna and Vronsky first encounter each other amid the ordinary business of arrivals and departures — a mundane setting made to carry disproportionate weight.
Levin's scenes of physical labor on his estate, mowing alongside his own peasants, which the novel treats with a seriousness and dignity unusual for its era's depictions of manual work.
The recurring image of trains and rail travel throughout the novel, tying together its most public settings and its characters' most private turns.
whatToNotice: Notice how the novel's famous opening sentence about happy and unhappy families sets up a comparative structure that the rest of the book keeps testing against its two central households.
Notice how differently Tolstoy handles interiority for Anna compared with Levin — track how much direct access to Levin's reasoning the narration grants versus how much it grants Anna.
Pay attention to scenes of physical work and physical sensation (mowing, skating, horse racing) and how much moral weight the novel invests in bodily activity.
Notice how often decisive emotional moments happen in transit — on trains, at stations, in carriages — rather than in settled domestic space.
Track the novel's treatment of Moscow versus the countryside as two different moral climates rather than simply two settings.
discussionQuestions: Why does Tolstoy structure the novel around two parallel households rather than telling a single unified story?
What does the novel's treatment of physical labor, especially in Levin's chapters, suggest about Tolstoy's developing views on how to live well?
How does free indirect style shape your sympathy for characters whose choices the novel does not otherwise endorse?
What role do public, transitional spaces like train stations play in a novel so concerned with private feeling?
furtherReading: Tolstoy's *War and Peace* — the earlier novel that established the scope and method *Anna Karenina* refines and compresses.
Gustave Flaubert's *Madame Bovary* — a near-contemporary European novel of marriage and adultery, often read against Tolstoy's very different treatment of similar material.
Vladimir Nabokov's lecture on Tolstoy in *Lectures on Russian Literature* — a close formal reading of Tolstoy's technique by a novelist who studied it closely.

title: The Garden Party
author: Katherine Mansfield
excerpt:
And after all the weather was ideal. They could not have had a more perfect day for a garden-party if they had ordered it. Windless, warm, the sky without a cloud. Only the blue was veiled with a haze of light gold, as it is sometimes in early summer. The gardener had been up since dawn, mowing the lawns and sweeping them, until the grass and the dark flat rosettes where the daisy plants had been seemed to shine. As for the roses, you could not help feeling they understood that roses are the only flowers that impress people at garden-parties; the only flowers that everybody is certain of knowing. Hundreds, yes, literally hundreds, had come out in a single night; the green bushes bowed down as though they had been visited by archangels.

Breakfast was not yet over before the men came to put up the marquee.

"Where do you want the marquee put, mother?"

"My dear child, it's no use asking me. I'm determined to leave everything to you children this year. Forget I am your mother. Treat me as an honoured guest."

But Meg could not possibly go and supervise the men. She had washed her hair before breakfast, and she sat drinking her coffee in a green turban, with a dark wet curl stamped on each cheek. Jose, the butterfly, always came down in a silk petticoat and a kimono jacket.

"You'll have to go, Laura; you're the artistic one."

Away Laura flew, still holding her piece of bread-and-butter. It's so delicious to have an excuse for eating out of doors, and besides, she loved having to arrange things; she always felt she could do it so much better than anybody else.

Four men in their shirt-sleeves stood grouped together on the garden path. They carried staves covered with rolls of canvas, and they had big tool-bags slung on their backs. They looked impressive. Laura wished now that she had not got the bread-and-butter, but there was nowhere to put it, and she couldn't possibly throw it away. She blushed and tried to look severe and even a little bit short-sighted as she came up to them.

"Good morning," she said, copying her mother's voice. But that sounded so fearfully affected that she was ashamed, and stammered like a little girl, "Oh--er--have you come--is it about the marquee?"

"That's right, miss," said the tallest of the men, a lanky, freckled fellow, and he shifted his tool-bag, knocked back his straw hat and smiled down at her. "That's about it."

His smile was so easy, so friendly that Laura recovered. What nice eyes he had, small, but such a dark blue! And now she looked at the others, they were smiling too. "Cheer up, we won't bite," their smile seemed to say. How very nice workmen were! And what a beautiful morning! She mustn't mention the morning; she must be business-like. The marquee.

"Well, what about the lily-lawn? Would that do?"

And she pointed to the lily-lawn with the hand that didn't hold the bread-and-butter. They turned, they stared in the direction. A little fat chap thrust out his under-lip, and the tall fellow frowned.

"I don't fancy it," said he. "Not conspicuous enough. You see, with a thing like a marquee," and he turned to Laura in his easy way, "you want to put it somewhere where it'll give you a bang slap in the eye, if you follow me."

Laura's upbringing made her wonder for a moment whether it was quite respectful of a workman to talk to her of bangs slap in the eye. But she did quite follow him.

"A corner of the tennis-court," she suggested. "But the band's going to be in one corner."

"H'm, going to have a band, are you?" said another of the workmen. He was pale. He had a haggard look as his dark eyes scanned the tennis-court. What was he thinking?

"Only a very small band," said Laura gently. Perhaps he wouldn't mind so much if the band was quite small. But the tall fellow interrupted.

"Look here, miss, that's the place. Against those trees. Over there. That'll do fine."

Against the karakas. Then the karaka-trees would be hidden. And they were so lovely, with their broad, gleaming leaves, and their clusters of yellow fruit. They were like trees you imagined growing on a desert island, proud, solitary, lifting their leaves and fruits to the sun in a kind of silent splendour. Must they be hidden by a marquee?

They must. Already the men had shouldered their staves and were making for the place. Only the tall fellow was left. He bent down, pinched a sprig of lavender, put his thumb and forefinger to his nose and snuffed up the smell. When Laura saw that gesture she forgot all about the karakas in her wonder at him caring for things like that--caring for the smell of lavender. How many men that she knew would have done such a thing? Oh, how extraordinarily nice workmen were, she thought. Why couldn't she have workmen for her friends rather than the silly boys she danced with and who came to Sunday night supper? She would get on much better with men like these.

It's all the fault, she decided, as the tall fellow drew something on the back of an envelope, something that was to be looped up or left to hang, of these absurd class distinctions. Well, for her part, she didn't feel them. Not a bit, not an atom... And now there came the chock-chock of wooden hammers. Some one whistled, some one sang out, "Are you right there, matey?" "Matey!" The friendliness of it, the--the--Just to prove how happy she was, just to show the tall fellow how at home she felt, and how she despised stupid conventions, Laura took a big bite of her bread-and-butter as she stared at the little drawing. She felt just like a work-girl.

"Laura, Laura, where are you? Telephone, Laura!" a voice cried from the house.

"Coming!" Away she skimmed, over the lawn, up the path, up the steps, across the veranda, and into the porch. In the hall her father and Laurie were brushing their hats ready to go to the office.

"I say, Laura," said Laurie very fast, "you might just give a squiz at my coat before this afternoon. See if it wants pressing."

"I will," said she. Suddenly she couldn't stop herself. She ran at Laurie and gave him a small, quick squeeze. "Oh, I do love parties, don't you?" gasped Laura.

"Ra-ther," said Laurie's warm, boyish voice, and he squeezed his sister too, and gave her a gentle push. "Dash off to the telephone, old girl."

The telephone. "Yes, yes; oh yes. Kitty? Good morning, dear. Come to lunch? Do, dear. Delighted of course. It will only be a very scratch meal--just the sandwich crusts and broken meringue-shells and what's left over. Yes, isn't it a perfect morning? Your white? Oh, I certainly should. One moment--hold the line. Mother's calling." And Laura sat back. "What, mother? Can't hear."

Mrs. Sheridan's voice floated down the stairs. "Tell her to wear that sweet hat she had on last Sunday."

"Mother says you're to wear that sweet hat you had on last Sunday. Good. One o'clock. Bye-bye."

Laura put back the receiver, flung her arms over her head, took a deep breath, stretched and let them fall. "Huh," she sighed, and the moment after the sigh she sat up quickly. She was still, listening. All the doors in the house seemed to be open. The house was alive with soft, quick steps and running voices. The green baize door that led to the kitchen regions swung open and shut with a muffled thud. And now there came a long, chuckling absurd sound. It was the heavy piano being moved on its stiff castors. But the air! If you stopped to notice, was the air always like this? Little faint winds were playing chase, in at the tops of the windows, out at the doors. And there were two tiny spots of sun, one on the inkpot, one on a silver photograph frame, playing too. Darling little spots. Especially the one on the inkpot lid. It was quite warm. A warm little silver star. She could have kissed it.

The front door bell pealed, and there sounded the rustle of Sadie's print skirt on the stairs. A man's voice murmured; Sadie answered, careless, "I'm sure I don't know. Wait. I'll ask Mrs Sheridan."

"What is it, Sadie?" Laura came into the hall.

"It's the florist, Miss Laura."

It was, indeed. There, just inside the door, stood a wide, shallow tray full of pots of pink lilies. No other kind. Nothing but lilies--canna lilies, big pink flowers, wide open, radiant, almost frighteningly alive on bright crimson stems.
